title: Problem Set 3
markdown:
## What this covers

This chapter is a problem set, not a lecture: Berkeley Stat243's "Problem Set 3", which recurs in
three offerings of the course (fall 2021, fall 2024, fall 2025) with the same two underlying goals
dressed in different languages and corpora. The first goal is to get hands-on experience with how a
large, real software package is put together internally — its namespace, and the chain of
`__init__.py` files that decides what `import`ing it actually makes available. The second is to
practice regular expressions and string processing by turning a corpus of real spoken transcripts
(US presidential debates, or presidents' State of the Union addresses) into structured per-speaker
statistics. It assumes the reader can already read the source tree of an installed package, knows
basic regex syntax, and — depending on the offering — has the HTML-scraping code from an earlier
problem set already in hand.

## How the assignment is shaped

Every offering pairs the same two problems with a third, lighter one. The package-internals problem
asks pointed questions about specific objects inside a widely used package — `statsmodels` in fall
2024, `pandas` in fall 2025 — tracing exactly which file each object is defined in, what kind of
object it is, and how the relevant `__init__.py` file(s) make it importable. The speech-processing
problem gives (or, in 2021, withholds) code that downloads and lightly cleans a set of transcripts,
and asks for the rest of the pipeline: splitting into per-speaker chunks, tokenizing, and computing
word/character statistics. The third problem is usually a design sketch: redo the speech-processing
solution's architecture in the *other* programming paradigm, without writing any code for it. Fall
2025 folds in an additional theme not present in the earlier offerings — explicit use of an AI
coding assistant, with the deliverable including the prompt used and a critique of what the
assistant got wrong — and adds a short, independent regex problem on detecting numeric literals.
Fall 2021 tacks on an unrelated closing problem: deliberately misusing an R language feature to
intercept console input.

Two practical hints recur across the package-internals problem, worth keeping regardless of which
package is being explored: `grep -R <pattern> <directory>` searches an entire source tree for a
name; and building an isolated environment (e.g. `conda create -n test_env python=3.12 statsmodels`)
lets you edit the *installed* package's files — comment out a line, add a print statement, set a
debugger breakpoint in an `__init__.py` — without touching anything else on the machine.

## Exercises

### 1. Package namespaces and imports

Two variants of the same investigation were assigned; pick whichever package you have to hand.

**`statsmodels` variant (fall 2024).**

a. Consider only `import statsmodels` on its own. What ends up in the `statsmodels` namespace this
   creates? Which module file stores the package's version number? What is the absolute path to the
   installed package on your machine?
b. The usual invocation is `import statsmodels.api as sm`. Describe, at the level of which files get
   read, what happens when this line runs. Then describe what kind of object `MICE` is, how it is
   imported, and where it is found — and do the same for `GLM`.
c. What is in the namespace of `sm.gam`? Describe how the importing works and in which modules the
   objects that appear there are actually defined.
d. What is `sm.distributions.monotone_fn_inverter` — is it a function, a class, or a class method?
   How is it imported, and in what file is it defined?

**`pandas` variant (fall 2025).**

After `import pandas`, for each of the following, say which namespace it (or its class) is in, what
file/module it is defined in, whether it is a function, a class, or a class method (naming the class
and any inheritance if so), and trace the `import` statement(s) in the relevant `__init__.py`
file(s) that put it where it is:

a. `pandas.core.config_init.is_terminal`
b. `pandas.read_csv`
c. `pandas.arrays.BooleanArray`
d. `pandas.DataFrame.to_csv`

### 2. Detecting numeric literals with regex (fall 2025)

a. Two AI-generated candidate regexes for detecting an integer or real number, positive or
   negative, were: `-?[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?` and `-?(\d+(\.\d+)?|\.\d+)`. What is the substantive
   difference between what the two would match? Is one better than the other?
b. Make the problem concrete: you are writing a CSV reader, and need to decide whether the text
   between two commas (with any surrounding quotes already stripped) is a number. Write a Python
   function that takes that text and returns either the detected numeric substring or `None`. It
   should catch plain reals such as `0.35`, `-.35`, `+72`; scientific notation such as `1.6e-8`
   (mantissa integer or real, exponent integer); and numbers using a thousands separator, such as
   `12,345.72` (which appears in a raw CSV field as `,"12,345.72",`). Everything else should be
   rejected. (Handling European-style numbers such as `12.345,73` as well is an optional extension,
   not a requirement.)
c. Build a test suite that covers a wide range of cases — an informal one, e.g. looping over a list
   of test strings and checking the results, is enough.

### 3. From transcript to structured speech data

The shared task, regardless of corpus: take a set of real spoken transcripts, strip out everything
that was not actually spoken, split what remains into chunks — one chunk per uninterrupted turn of
speech by one speaker, merging consecutive chunks from the same speaker — and compute per-speaker
statistics from the result.

Two corpora were used:

- **Presidential debates** (fall 2024, fall 2025): transcripts of the 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016
  and 2020 US presidential debates, from the Commission on Presidential Debates website, chosen to
  cover domestic-policy content so that debate topic is roughly controlled for. Both offerings
  supply the HTML-downloading and initial-processing code (`ps3prob3.py`) so the exercise is purely
  about processing text already in hand.
- **State of the Union addresses** (fall 2021): the run of presidents' annual addresses to Congress,
  from the American Presidency Project (UCSB). Unlike the debate version, here the downloading step
  is also part of the exercise — scraping an index page for the individual speech URLs before
  processing each one — so the whole pipeline, start to finish, is self-contained in the solution.

Common sub-tasks, whichever corpus you use:

a. Get each transcript into your working language and, if it is not already, split it into
   individual speeches and, within a speech, the spoken chunks (dropping non-spoken annotations such
   as "(Laughter)" and "(Applause)" — or, for the State of the Union version, counting rather than
   discarding how often each occurs). Report the number of chunks per speaker.
b. Tokenize the chunks into individual words. An existing NLP tokenizer is a reasonable choice for
   this; regular expressions are also acceptable, particularly if you want more practice with them.
   Perfect accuracy on spoken text is not expected.
c. For each speaker (and, in the debate version, for each debate), count words and characters and
   compute average word length; compare across speakers and, where you have several years of data,
   over time.
d. Check your functions against a few simple, deliberately easy test inputs. A formal test framework
   is not required for this.

Extra credit, all versions: count occurrences of a fixed list of politically loaded words and word
stems — I, we, America{,n}, democra{cy,tic}, republic, Democrat{,ic}, Republican, free{,dom},
terror{,ism} (2021 instead counts *war* and *God*, keeping "God Bless" separate), safe{,r,st,ty},
{Jesus, Christ, Christian} — and produce at least one plot commenting on what you find. The 2021
version additionally asks for a plot of how these quantities changed over time, and whether they
differ between Republican and Democratic presidents from Franklin Roosevelt onward.

The fall 2025 version reframes this whole exercise around working with an AI coding assistant end
to end: you must understand every line of the assistant's code before submitting it, and in addition

- record the prompt you used to start the interaction;
- describe specific errors, minor or major, the assistant made (the assignment itself notes one
  concrete case: the assistant used to write it merged consecutive same-speaker chunks incorrectly);
- note anything you learned about Python from examining the generated code; and
- reflect on the overall experience — whether the code worked well, how much you had to change
  either yourself or by iterating with the assistant, any unfamiliar syntax you had to look up, and
  whether this style of working felt more efficient than writing the code yourself.

### 4. Sketch the complementary design

Whichever paradigm you used to solve the speech-processing exercise, sketch — design only, do not
write any code — a solution in the *other* one.

- If your solution was object-oriented, design a functional-programming version: for each function
  you would need, list its inputs and its output, and briefly comment on its purpose.
- If your solution was functional, design an object-oriented version: for each class you would need,
  list its fields and its methods, briefly commenting on the purpose of each, and note where a
  method relies on other fields or methods.

### 5. Hijacking the console's quit keystroke (fall 2021)

a. Suppose you want typing `k` at the R or RStudio console to quit R immediately, with no
   confirmation prompt. What R function call, with what argument, quits R without asking any
   questions? What sequence of steps does R actually carry out when you type `k` and press enter,
   and how could you arrange for your quit call to run instead? (Keep this code in a chunk that does
   not evaluate when the document is knitted — if it works, it will quit R before knitting finishes.)
b. Now try to achieve the same thing by typing `q` instead of `k`. Does it work? If so, explain how
   your version of `q` and R's own `q()` function manage to coexist.

## Sources

- `docs/statistical-computing/berkeley/stat243/fall-2024/ps/ps3.md` — converted losslessly from
  `ps/ps3.qmd` in the berkeley-stat243 fall-2024 repository, CC BY 4.0. Problems 1–3: the
  `statsmodels` namespace investigation, the presidential-debate chunking exercise, and the FP/OOP
  design sketch.
- `docs/statistical-computing/berkeley/stat243/fall-2025/ps/ps3.md` — converted losslessly from
  `ps/ps3.qmd` in the berkeley-stat243 fall-2025 repository, CC BY 4.0. Problems 1–3: the
  numeric-literal regex exercise, the `pandas` namespace investigation, and the AI-assisted
  presidential-debate exercise.
- `docs/statistical-computing/berkeley/stat243/stat243-fall-2021/ps/ps3.md` — model-reconstructed
  from a PDF with no text layer (berkeley-stat243 stat243-fall-2021 repository, CC0-1.0); its source
  note flags the prose as a paraphrase and every detail as unverified. Problems 1–3: the State of
  the Union speech-processing exercise (in R), the OOP design sketch, and the console
  quit-hijacking exercise. Treat exact wording and word lists from this file as a pointer to the
  original PDF rather than settled fact.
- Referred to but not contained in any of the three files: the course's Unit 5 material on package
  structure, which all three problem sets assume has already been covered; Problem Set 1, for the
  formatting (and, in 2024, attribution) requirements each version points back to; the `ps3prob3.py`
  download/preprocessing script supplied separately in each course's GitHub repository; the source
  code of `statsmodels`, `pandas`, and R itself; and the transcripts themselves, at debates.org (the
  Commission on Presidential Debates) and the American Presidency Project (UCSB).
